title: HBO Lands Hot Drama Spec ‘Imposter’ By DWA Assistant Kalos Chu With Lauren LeFranc Producing
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie Kenan Thompson To Fill In For Simon Cowell As Guest Judge On ‘America’s Got Talent’ ‘Stuart Fails’ Stars Kevin Sussman & Lauren Lapkus Reveal Filming Episode 6 Scene “Was Terrifying” ‘Manifest’ Spinoff ‘Arrivals’ Ordered By Netflix View All August 31, 2026 9:30am Kalos Chu and Lauren LeFranc Courtesy/Getty From an assistant desk to a premium HBO development deal: thousands of aspiring writers dream of making that leap. For one, Kalos Chu — who serendipitously works at DreamWorks Animation — that dream became a reality. After a bidding war for his spec Imposter , which started with 10 offers before the field was narrowed down to a three-way battle between HBO, Netflix and Amazon, the drama project landed at HBO for development with an option for a writers room to follow. The Penguin creator/showrunner Lauren LeFranc will executive produce via her banner Acid and Tender Productions under her overall deal at HBO, with her head of TV and fill Rachel Jacobs also exec producing. Related Stories News Everything We Know About 'The Gilded Age' Season 4 So Far Cancellations and Renewals NFL Films & HBO's 'Hard Knocks: Offseason' Set For 2027 Return, Replacing 'In-Season' Edition Written and executive produced by Chu, Imposter is a dark mystery that follows an outsider entering his freshman year at an elite university. Watch on Deadline This is the first writing credit for Chu, a 2023 Harvard graduate with a BA degree in English. “After graduation, I hope to pursue a career in screenwriting — a passion that has developed, in large part, due to my experience in the English department,” he wrote in a 2023 essay about his college tenure. While Imposter makes Chu’s Hollywood writing debut, he had been preparing for it for years. Starting in fall 2020, Chu did a string of stints as a development intern, at Atlas Entertainment, Voltage Pictures, Day Zero Productions, Nickelodeon Animation and DreamWorks Animation. In summer 2022, he interned in physical production at Lucasfilm, to, as he put it in the 2023 essay, address gaps in his filmmaking knowledge of how, exactly, a movie is made and “the practical constraints that screenwriters must grapple with.” A year after graduation, Chu got a job as a feature development assistant at DreamWorks Animation where he has been for the past two years, writing Imposter i n his spare time. With the script selling, Chu will be leaving his DWA job and is currently helping find a replacement. As of now, he doesn’t have an agent; that will likely change soon, too. The Shane Gillis sitcom has been renewed for Season 4 at Netflix, a few weeks after the third season premiered on the streamer. Hailing from co-creators Gillis, John McKeever and Steve Gerben, “Tires” follows the dysfunctional staff of auto repair chain Valley Forge. The workplace comedy started as a scrappy passion project — Gillis uploaded a pilot to YouTube in 2019 before the trio financed and produced a six-episode first season independently in Pennsylvania. Netflix picked up the show for distribution in 2024 and then renewed and funded future seasons. Related Stories Shannon Wallace, Curtiss Cook, Lauren E. Banks, Liv Symone, Jason Dirden Join Starz Black Rodeo Drama 'The Witcher' Co-Producer Rae Benjamin to Receive Starz #TakeTheLead Award at Humanitas Event, Presented by Russell T Davies “Tires” stars Gillis, Gerben Chris O’Connor, Kilah Fox, Stavros Halkias and Thomas Haden Church. Guest stars include Andrew Schulz, Jamie Lynn Sigler, Billy Magnussen, Taylor Misiak, Sofia Hasmik, Bobby Lee, Dan Soder, Rachel Blanchard, Garret Dillahunt, Anjelica Bette Fellini, Matt Walsh, Tommy Pope, Steph Tolev and H. Foley. Popular on Variety Earlier this year, Variety broke the news that Gillis and McKeever had inked a creative partnership with Netflix to develop new shows and movies. The deal also includes two new stand-up specials from Gillis. Delivering a short and sweet quote about the “Tires” renewal, Gillis said, “It’s cool to get to make another season of ‘Tires.'” McKeever was a tiny bit more expressive: “I love this show and everyone who works on it. Since its 2024 debut, “Tires” has amassed more than 45 million views across three seasons. “‘Tires’ continues to deliver the unapologetic comedy and authentic point of view Shane, John and Steve’s fans know and love, and Season 3 hitting its highest-ever Top 10 ranking proves this fandom just keeps growing,” said Tracey Pakosta, Netflix’s vice president of U.S. comedy. “We love working with this team and can’t wait to see what’s next for the Valley Forge crew in Season 4.” The show is executive produced by Gillis, Gerben and McKeever; Brandon James for Rough House; Brian Stern and Kenneth Slotnick for AGI Entertainment Media & Management; and Becky Astphan. McKeever is the director, and he writes alongside Gillis, Gerben, Chris O’Connor, Amy McLeish, Bobby Telatovich, Sam Mazany, Bobby Telatovich, Amy McLeish-Milligan, Sam Mazany and Grace Cohen. Over the past few years, Gillis has become one of the biggest comedians in the world. In May, he hosted Netflix’s “The Roast of Kevin Hart,” and in July, he sold 76,212 tickets to his stadium show at Lincoln Financial Field, breaking the Guinness World Record for most tickets sold for a solo comedy show. title: ‘Off Campus’ Launches Halloween Costumes Including Briar University Jerseys and Varsity Jackets
full_text: If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission. Briar University is getting dressed for Halloween. Spirit Halloween is bringing Prime Video’s breakout romance series “ Off Campus ” into costume aisles this fall, launching an officially licensed collection inspired by some of the show’s most recognizable looks. SHOP ONLINE The lineup lets fans dress like they’ve stepped onto the fictional college campus, with Briar U hockey jerseys and varsity jackets alongside more character-specific pieces. Among them are the bunny costume worn by Wesley at the duo birthday party and the dress Allie wears for her Jennifer Lopez costume. Based on Elle Kennedy’s bestselling five-book romance series , the college soap follows the players on Briar University’s elite hockey team and the women in their lives as they navigate relationships, friendship and early adulthood. STREAM ‘OFF CAMPUS’ Season 1, which premiered May 13, centers on music student Hannah Wells, played by Ella Bright, and star hockey player Garrett Graham, played by Belmont Cameli. The two strike a deal — she’ll tutor him, he’ll help her catch the attention of another guy — that predictably gets more complicated when their fake arrangement starts producing real feelings. The adaptation quickly proved that Kennedy’s BookTok-era fan base could translate to streaming. Amazon says the series drew 36 million viewers worldwide during its first 12 days, making it the third-most-watched debut season of a Prime Video series, behind only “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” and “Fallout.” Prime Video has already renewed the show for Season 2, which will shift its primary romance to Allie Hayes (Mika Abdalla) and Dean Di Laurentis (Stephen Kalyn), whose relationship began taking shape during the first season. title: Danny Boyle Set to Receive the Creative Impact in Directing Award from Variety at Venice Film Festival
full_text: Aug 31, 2026 9:16am PT Danny Boyle Set to Receive the Creative Impact in Directing Award from Variety at Venice Film Festival By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest Danny Boyle Set to Receive the Creative Impact in Directing Award from Variety at Venice Film Festival 34 minutes ago Isabelle Huppert Vampire Film ‘The Blood Countess’ Bought for North America (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Venice Film Festival Maintains Jury Press Conference After Solving ‘Scheduling Issues’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All WireImage Variety will honor Oscar-winning British filmmaker Danny Boyle with its Creative Impact in Directing Award at the Venice Film Festival on Tuesday. Boyle, whose wide-ranging credits span “Trainspotting,” “Slumdog Millionaire,” “Steve Jobs” and the “28 Days Later” franchise, will receive the award during Variety ’s Venice pre-opening night party at the Hotel Excelsior on the Lido. Related Stories San Sebastián Co-Production Forum: Celina Murga, Mariana Rondón, Matias Mariani, Santiago Loza and Christopher Murray Among Selected Naomi Watts to Be Honored at San Sebastián Film Festival Boyle’s next film “Ink,” a drama about the birth of Rupert Murdoch’s tabloid empire, will kick off the festival on Sept. 2. Popular on Variety “From changing independent film with ‘Trainspotting’ to winning the Oscar for ‘Slumdog Millionaire’ to terrifying audiences with the ’28 Days Later’ franchise, Danny Boyle has inspired, entertained and transported us with his singular vision of storytelling,“ said Ramin Setoodeh, Variety’ s co-editor-in-chief and co-president. “His new film, ‘Ink,’ starring Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce and Claire Foy, will be one of this fall’s great discoveries. We are thrilled to honor him with Variety’s Creative Impact Award for directing at the Venice Film Festival.“ “Ink” Venice Film Festival Boyle will be joined at the Venice event by “Ink” stars O’Connell, Pearce and Foy, as well as Graham and producers Tracey Seaward, Tessa Ross and Michael Ellenberg, alongside Venice Film Festival artistic director Alberto Barbera and members of the jury. Previous recipients of Variety’s Creative Impact in Directing Award include Guillermo Del Toro and Jacques Audiard. Boyle most recently returned to the zombie franchise “28 Days Later,” directing “28 Years Later” and serving as a producer on its follow-up, “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple.” Boyle previously won the directing Oscar for “Slumdog Millionaire,” which became one of the rare films to sweep the Academy Awards, BAFTAs and Golden Globes as well as the PGA and DGA prizes for best picture and directing. “Ink“ is based on James Graham’s Tony and Olivier Award-winning play about the period in 1969 when Murdoch and editor Larry Lamb transformed British tabloid journalism. The film will open in select theaters Dec. 11 before streaming on Netflix on Jan. 8 in the U.S. and Latin America. Following Venice, it will make its Canadian debut at the Toronto International Film Festival. Studiocanal handles worldwide sales and will release the film theatrically starting in January across its territories. title: Dolly Parton Estate Announces 2027 Dollyfest Shows in Nashville, London
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All August 31, 2026 9:08am Dolly Parton performs on stage at The Dominion Theatre on March 29th, 1983 in London, United Kingdom. Pete Still/Redferns/Getty Images Dolly Parton ‘s estate announced a two-day, two-country music festival called “Dollyfest” on Monday, set to honor the late country legend sometime in 2027. Parton’s estate said Monday that Dollyfest was originally slated to take place in January of 2026, around when Parton turned 80, with the singer-songwriter planning on performing and hosting. With Parton now gone, the event will “now morph into a global double-day, double-weekend, double-continent party of a lifetime,” her estate said, with one date in Nashville and a second in London. Related Stories Music Stars Gather at Grand Ole Opry for Dolly Parton Musical Tribute: "Most Beloved Human Being in the World" TV 'Entertainment Tonight' Presents New Dolly Parton TV Special: Where to Watch Online “What Dolly started, we will ensure is brought to life,” Danny Nozell, Founder and CEO of CTK Enterprises and Parton’s longtime manager, said in a statement. “Many people behind the scenes know that DOLLYFEST is a dream of Dolly’s that was intended to take place on her 80th birthday in Nashville. We had the venue booked and we had the announcement ready to go. And then, in August 2025, Dolly had to take a step back after her initial health challenges. A lot of people always say, WWDD (What Would Dolly Do?), and, well, at this moment, DOLLYFEST is WDWD (What Dolly Would Do!).” Parton’s estate announced Dollyfest about a week after Parton died on August 25 after a battle with cancer. One of the most beloved celebrities of all time, her passing inspired a tidal wave of tributes from around the world, with Parton remembered not just for her music but for her acting career, decades of philanthropy and advocacy. “We are not discouraging people from celebrating Dolly in the ways they choose,” Nozell said. “However, as far as a traditional memorial goes, that is not something Dolly wanted. So, instead, it feels more appropriate for us to take a beat, let all the tributes that immediately make sense occur naturally, and then, see through this festival-style concept that was truly dreamed up by Dolly. This is something that is authentic to her, something that feels right to me, and something that artists and fans around the world can participate in, while also giving everyone time to grieve, and giving everyone time to plan.” The estate said information on tickets and the shows’ dates is forthcoming. title: Messi Reveals Argentinian National Team Retirement; Will Still Play For MLS’ Inter Miami

In a post, the 2022 World Cup champion made his long anticipated second exit from the national team official. “Time is running short, chapters come to a close, and this is one that hurts me deeply,” Messi wrote six weeks after his Argentina were defeated 1-0 in overtime at the 2026 World Cup Final by Spain. “I love, have loved, and will always love being part of the national team,” he added. Messi had previously retired from playing for Argentina in 2016, but un-retired in time for the 2018 World Cup, where the team was booted out of the Round 16 by France (who went on to win the Final that year). In addition to what was going on in the World Cup, Messi’s father was ill during the tournament. A close advisor to his record breaking son, Jorge Messi died on August 8 at the age of 68. title: Marty Nadler, Writer, Producer and Longtime Garry Marshall Contributor, Dies at 80
full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All August 31, 2026 9:00am Marty Nadler Courtesy of Charlie Nadler Marty Nadler, the writer, producer and stand-up comedian who collaborated with Garry Marshall on projects including Happy Days , Laverne & Shirley , Pretty Woman and Runaway Bride for more than four decades, has died. He was 80. Nadler died Wednesday in Margate, Florida, of complications from the autoimmune disorder myasthenia gravis, his son, Charlie Nadler, announced. Starting in the 1970s, Nadler served as lead writer on several sitcoms produced by fellow Bronx native Marshall, including Who’s Watching the Kids and Blansky’s Beauties , and warmed up the audience on many of those shows as well. Related Stories TV Jackie Glass, 'Swift Justice' Host, Dies at 70 Lifestyle Anna Louizos, Scenic Designer for Broadway's 'In the Heights,' 'School of Rock' and 'Avenue Q,' Dies at 69 He contributed jokes to nine Marshall films, among them Pretty Woman (1990), Frankie and Johnny (1991), Runaway Bride (1999), The Princess Diaries 2: Royal Engagement (2004), Valentine’s Day (2010) and Mother’s Day (2016). Marshall considered Nadler a good luck charm and gave him a cameo in those movies. Away from his pal, Nader also worked on such TV comedies as That’s My Mama , Chico and the Man , The Last Resort , Love, Sidney , She’s the Sheriff , The Redd Foxx Show , Perfect Strangers , The Hogan Family and Amen . Martin Nadler was born in the Bronx on Oct. 13, 1945. His father, Max, was a traveling salesman who died when Nadler was 3, so he was raised by his mother, Betty, who had immigrated from Russia. “I was always funny in class. I was always in the school plays,” he said in a 2024 intervew. “When I was eight years old, I decided I wanted to go into showbiz.” Nadler honed his comedy chops as a summer camp counselor and discovered a passion for stand-up while a theater major at Ithaca College. He returned to New York City after college, pursued acting and became a regular at The Improv, where he got to know the likes of Jay Leno, Richard Lewis and Jimmie Walker and became known as a “comic’s comic.” On New Year’s Eve, he would portray the New Year’s baby, bursting in from a freezing night clad in a diaper. Jeffrey Kramer, a college friend who had become an actor — he played the deputy sheriff Hendricks in the first two Jaws films — introduced Nadler to The Vineyard Players, a summer stock troupe on Martha’s Vineyard. After one performance, Penny Marshall came backstage with then-husband Rob Reiner and offered to help him if he ever came west. When he did, the future Laverne & Shirley star picked him up at the airport, put him up for a few weeks and introduced him to her brother Garry. He read a spec script that Nadler wrote, beginning their relationship. When Nadler was writing for Laverne & Shirley in 1976, he met a writer named Holly Mascott, who came to Paramount to pitch him story ideas, and he gave her a script assignment. They would marry on Martha’s Vineyard in 1978 and buy a home there in 1984. Nadler retired to South Florida in the early aughts and was an executive producer of iMordecai (2022), starring Judd Hirsch. Several years ago, after Charlie became a writer and comedian of his own, he invited his dad to perform onstage one night. That began a father-son collaboration that took them to theaters around the country. They recently recorded their act at the Garry Marshall Theatre in Burbank. Titled A Boomer & a Millennial Walk Into a Special , it will be released early next year by Comedy Dynamics (it was their last performance together). “It was a magical evening, with family, friends and colleagues from all chapters of dad’s life in attendance,” Charlie said. Survivors also include Mascott — she and Nadler remained close after their divorce in 2002 — and his daughter-in-law, Cary Kandel. Nadler will be interned on Martha’s Vineyard, and celebrations of life in multiple locations are being planned. Donations in his memory can be made to the Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America . title: ‘Onslaught’ Review: Adria Arjona Shines in Adam Wingard’s Intriguingly Colorful, Ultimately Underwhelming Action Thriller
full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All August 31, 2026 9:00am Adria Arjona in 'Onslaught.' Richard Foreman/A24 If nothing else, Onslaught stands as proof that director Adam Wingard , making his way back to lean, mean originals after a decade in the IP mines, hasn’t lost his touch for the sort of deliciously vivid details that suggest motherlodes of stories unto themselves. In the first few minutes alone, we get grinning jack-o’-lanterns lined up in a dusty canyon, exploding one by one in target practice. A knife slicing through gnarled, unpeeled carrots that look like nothing so much as human fingers. An ancient Nazi scientist ( Dan Stevens ) crawling across a carpet to lick a woman’s stilettoed foot. Related Stories TV Dan Stevens Cast as RoboCop in Prime Video's Reboot TV Netflix's 'Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story' Trailer Teases Ella Beatty, Charlie Hunnam, Rebecca Hall in Bloody Tale of Infamous Ax Murders Onslaught The Bottom Line Tons of promise, not quite enough payoff. Release date: Friday, Sep. 4 Cast: Adria Arjona, Blake Kennedy, Reginald VelJohnson, Eric Wareheim, Dan Stevens, Michael Biehn, Rebecca Hall Director: Adam Wingard Screenwriters: Adam Wingard, Simon Barrett Rated R, 1 hour 32 minutes Each image lands as a promise — an amuse-bouche for the veritable feast of ultraviolence sure to come once all these disparate elements start to crash and burn into one another. But building anticipatory buzz is one thing; paying it off is another. Gloriously crafted if narratively undercooked, the action-thriller is a pretty good time. It’s just that it had seemed for a moment like it was going to be a great one. The pumpkin shooter turns out to be Celeste ( Adria Arjona ), a former Army sniper with the shaky hands, extensive gun collection and dirty-dish-filled sink of someone barely keeping it together. Wracked with PTSD, she’s retreated in her civilian life into a remote desert trailer park populated by other mild eccentrics who seem more comfortable removed from the rest of the world, including a kindly Vietnam vet (Reginald VelJohnson as Josiah) and a bitter drunk of a cop (Eric Wareheim as Kovacks). But the relative safety of Windy Oasis is violated when a trio of super-soldiers escape from a top-secret military bunker up the road. As these experiments, described to one eager businessman as “the human equivalent of heat-seeking missiles,” close in, Celeste must take up arms to protect herself, her young daughter (Blake Kennedy’s Daisy) and her community. In other words: Expect a home invasion thriller, of the sort Wingard made his name on in 2011’s You’re Next and 2014’s The Guest . On that front, Onslaught delivers well enough. Between the soldiers’ imperviousness to bullets, immunity to pain and indifference to conscience, it doesn’t take long before they rack up a body count in the dozens — chopping through walls and punching through windows and blowing off heads with cold, mechanical relentlessness. Fine craftsmanship can be seen on every level of the action. Nick Interlandi’s soundscapes swell with the rat-a-tat of machine guns, or zero in on the precise, satisfying crunch of glass cracking under bone, while Oren Soffer’s cinematography runs the gamut from sickly clinical to startlingly sensual. And yet, the second half of the movie can’t feel like something of a letdown — as if Wingard, having shown us all the cool shiny toys he has at his disposal, has forgotten to come up with anything to do with them beyond smash them together. Stevens’ Kammler makes a big immediate impression as a pervy little freak, but then gets less room than you might hope to swan around in his snow-white capes. Rebecca Hall , playing his elegantly domineering wife, gets even less. Deep into the second act, Drew Starkey has an all-timer of an intro as elite operative Cyrus, the camera practically caressing his bare torso as he rolls on molly and ogles G-string-clad women in a sex club. But I’d be hard-pressed to say what the character actually accomplishes beyond stand around various scenes of carnage; at one point, in fact, he’s explicitly instructed not to do anything at all. The political themes hinted at by the opening collage — clips of robot soldiers and photos of Abu Ghraib torture victims and headlines about the U.S. embrace of Nazi scientists after World War II, all conspiring to remind us that the American military has always been capable of profound horror — never completely fade from view. But they never really get fleshed out any further, either. The potential to tap into the ambient paranoia of our current militarized age goes unfulfilled. What Onslaught does remember to develop are the good guys, far less colorful than the villains but, in their down-to-earth relatability, no less compelling. Celeste should be another feather in the cap for Arjona, a wonderfully versatile actor who’s been steadily on the rise for the past few years. Here, she gets to glower and shoot and make a bloody mess with the best of the action-hero badasses. But she also gets to demonstrate the humor and warmth that’s made her such a delight in films like Hit-Man . She’s especially winsome in her scenes with Josiah, the two grizzled vets teasing each other or coming to each other’s aid with the unspoken kinship that comes from shared experience. It’s his unassuming decency, even more than Daisy’s sweet innocence or Celeste’s mama-bear toughness, that makes Windy Oasis feel like a world worth saving. One only wishes the film could have done the same while also making a fully satisfying meal of the cartoonish villains who’ve come to destroy them. Full credits Distributor: A24 Production companies: A24, Lyrical Media, Recorded Picture Company, Breakaway Civilization Productions, 828 Productions Cast: Adria Arjona, Blake Kennedy, Reginald VelJohnson, Eric Wareheim, Dan Stevens, Michael Biehn, Rebecca Hall Director: Adam Wingard Screenwriters: Adam Wingard, Simon Barrett Producers: Simon Barrett, Andrew Swett, Alexander Black, Jeremy Platt Executive producers: David Kern, Jon Rosenberg, Natalie Sellars, Stuart Manashil, Todd Lundbohm Director of photography: Oren Soffer Production designer: Tom Hammock Costume designer: Alexis Forte Editors: Josh Schaeffer, Adam Avery Music: Matthew Pusti Sound design: Nick Interlandi Casting director: Rebecca Dealy Rated R, 1 hour 32 minutes THR

title: Leonardo DiCaprio’s Appian Way and Dax Dasilva Board Soleil Moon Frye’s Shifty Shellshock Doc
full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All August 31, 2026 9:00am Soleil Moon Frye is pictured with Shifty Shellshock on the beach. Credit: Amanda Demme/Courtesy of Subject Soleil Moon Frye ‘s documentary Werewolf in the Waves , an intimate look at her relationship with late Crazy Town rocker Shifty Shellshock, has a new team riding the surf with her. Leonardo DiCaprio ‘s Appian Way and Emmy winner Dax Dasilva have boarded as executive producers. Frye, who previously directed the nostalgia-laced doc Kid 90 about her experience in Hollywood as a child star turned young adult in the 1990s, directed the majority of Werewolf in the Waves on her iPhone. The footage she captured centers on a reunion with Seth Binzer, aka Shifty, an old friend from childhood. Frye originally set out to document Crazy Town’s comeback tour — the band had a monster smash with “Butterfly” back in the day — until that connection evolved to a love story. However, as sparks were flying, Binzer relapsed on drugs, a tragic spiral that changed the trajectory of the film and his life as he died from an accidental overdose in the summer of 2024. Related Stories TV 'Furious' Renewed for Second Season at Hulu TV 'The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives' Season 5 Trailer Teases Leadup to Taylor Frankie Paul's 'Bachelorette' Season Being Pulled Frye directed the film, which has already played at some film festivals. She serves as an executive producer alongside Appian Way’s Jennifer Davisson and Phillip Watson, Dasilva and Binzer’s sisters, Aubrey Binzer and Mieke Binzer Dumont. Frye and Appian Way previously worked together on Kid 90 , which streamed on Hulu . “Having Dax join us as an executive producer feels incredibly meaningful,” said Frye of the producer, entrepreneur and philanthropist who won an Emmy for outstanding nature documentary for Wildcat . “His heart, vision and passion for this story mean so much to me, and I am thrilled that he is helping us carry Seth’s legacy forward.” She continued: “Seth’s dream was to share his journey with the world, to help those struggling with addiction and mental health challenges feel less alone and to create greater understanding and compassion. I am forever grateful for my children, Seth’s sisters, our loved ones and everyone who stood beside us throughout this journey. It is my sincere hope that this film inspires meaningful conversations and reminds us to meet one another with greater empathy, compassion and understanding.” Per the filmmakers, Dasilva’s involvement is part of an ongoing commitment to doc and impact-driven storytelling, following such work as Wildcat and the environmental doc Yanuni . He serves as a producer on the upcoming Jane Goodall documentary Just Me, Jane. He’s also the founder of the global commerce platform Lightspeed Commerce and Age of Union, a nonprofit dedicated to conservation initiatives through film, media and cultural engagement. “As an impact-producer searching for deeply personal and inspiring stories that will reach audiences and create change, I was struck by Werewolf in the Waves ,” he said in a statement. “Soleil Moon Frye’s unfiltered perspective on addiction and loss connects to the resilience, heart and love at the center of so many stories for the millions of Americans who have been personally impacted by drug addiction. I hope through this story others can understand addiction more closely, find more empathy and love for those facing these hurdles and join the film’s final call to seek help if you or someone you know is hurting.” In addition to Werewolf in the Waves and Kid 90 , Frye directed The Carters: Hurts to Love You , a two-parter about the Carter family (siblings Nick, Aaron and Angel) and their journey through fame amid mental health, addiction and other challenges. She’s repped by CAA and Tyler Kroos at Kroos Entertainment Group. THR

title: Sony Aims to Connect Advertisers to PlayStation Users With Launch of ‘Live TV on PS5’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Aug 31, 2026 9:00am PT Sony Aims to Connect Advertisers to PlayStation Users With Launch of ‘Live TV on PS5’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Antonia Hylton’s New MS NOW Weekend Show ‘The Assignment’ Debuts September 12 2 hours ago DraftKings Taps Kevin Hart, Nick Jonas for Road-Trip Commercial That Touts Wagering, Predictions 7 hours ago President Trump Calls For FCC Punishment of NBC News’ Kristen Welker Following Promotional ‘Meet the Press’ Banter 23 hours ago See All Courtesy of Sony The audience that gravitates to games on PlayStation has become notoriously difficult for advertisers to reach. Until now. Sony Pictures Television on Monday unveiled “Live TV on PS5,” an offering of more than 100 free ad-supported video channels that can all be accessed via the PlayStation 5 console. The service is initially available in the U.S., with Canada expected to follow. Sony expects the package to evolve over time, with new channels, themed programming and live events added as warranted. Related Stories ‘Outlander: Blood of My Blood’ Season 2 Trailer: Scottish Uprising Threatens 'Outlander' Prequel 'The Witcher' Co-Producer Rae Benjamin to Receive Starz #TakeTheLead Award at Humanitas Event, Presented by Russell T Davies Sony, which owns PlayStation, will make the service available via its Bravia television consoles later this year. Popular on Variety In some ways, Sony is offering a lifeline to reach a group of consumers who have been among the first to cut the proverbial cord connecting them to traditional TV services. “When you look at sort of the habits and behaviors of this community, they are gaming and engaging with video and they’re probably not showing up in other connected TV environments often,” says Peter Wood, executive vice president of consumer platforms and services at Sony Pictures Entertainment, during a recent interview. Sony’s FAST forward move is emblematic of a broader shift taking place in the media sector, where the heady days of streaming are quickly giving way to more focused efforts to forge connections between content and the people who might consume it. Sony has sold more than 95 million PlayStation 5 units around the world as of June 30, according to data from Sony Interactive Entertainment, but the device’s users aren’t likely to be found through the typical kinds of outreach. More traditional media outlets and new-tech counterparts are testing a variety of free ad-supported methods that may be better suited for specific audience niches than the mass subscriber bases sought by Netflix, Peacock or HBO Max, among others. The offering will feature programming from ABC News, A+E Global Media, AMC Global Media, Amazon MGM Studios, ESPN, Fox, Lionsgate, NASCAR, NBCUniversal, NFL Channel, Radial Entertainment and UFC, among others. Channels included are ABC News Live; Fox Sports, Fox Weather and LiveNOW from Fox;; NBC News Now and NBC Sports Now; and NFL Channel. The package will also include content from eCLUTCH ,an esports broadcaster; Spotify’s The Ringer; and channels dedicated specifically to “Community” and “The Shield” as well as Sony One’s Action Hits and Horror Hits. Two anime channels from Crunchyroll, also part of Sony, have been created exclusively for Live TV. And viewers will be able to watch series including “Hot Ones,” “Wicked Tuna,” and “The Walking Dead,” along with selected movies such as “The Hunger Games,” “Hancock,” and “Resident Evil.” Sony executives have been intent for years on trying to find ways to stitch the company’s assets together to help advertisers reach crowds of consumers they desire, says Wood. Sony engages with tens of millions of customers around the world across our devices,” he says. “I don’t think it’s rocket science to look at trying to remove the friction of content discovery across different media.” Sony will work with both Publica and PubMatic, two companies that focus on connected-TV advertising, and Wood expects interest will be high if the commercials that are served are meaningful to PlayStation’s users. “This audience appeals to everyone,” he says. “We are just being very thoughtful” about ensuring the advertising presented is “relevant.” ‘One Night Only’ Review: Monica Barbaro and Callum Turner Are Too Hot for This Sexless Sex Comedy New Radicals’ Gregg Alexander Soft-Relaunches Band With ‘One Night Only’ Movie Song Ahead of Their First Album in 28 Years ‘Neuromancer’ First Look: Callum Turner Is a Cyberspace Criminal in Teaser for Apple TV Sci-Fi Series Loading comments... title: ‘Furious’ Finale: Emmy Rossum and Creator Elizabeth Meriwether on That Final Shot, Who Killed Isabel and How Alice’s Decisions Will Affect Season 2
full_text: Disney SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers from “Hart Island,” the Season 1 finale of “ Furious ,” now streaming on Hulu. So what’s the deal with Alice’s little smile at the end of “Furious”? Emmy Rossum ’s pleased expression, as happy as we’ve seen Alice throughout “Furious,” is the final image that she and series creator Elizabeth Meriwether deliver to the audience. Not forever, though: Hulu announced last week that “Furious” has been renewed for Season 2. The smile is in answer to a question posed by Catherine (Lola Petticrew), the serial killer Alice has hunted all season in her capacity as an FBI agent. Earlier in the season, Catherine gave Alice a pep talk about how wonderful it feels to kill men who prey upon women and girls. Now imprisoned, and having figured out that Alice murdered the Jeffrey Epstein-coded predator Jay Easton (Peter McRobbie), Catherine asks insistently, “I said , did you like the way it felt?” The Season 1 finale mostly takes place at the Easton estate in Connecticut, after Alice essentially sends Catherine there at the end of the previous episode. Emma Easton (Hope Davis) has put her father, Jay, who’s whining about his predicament, to bed, and plots with FBI special agent Ed George (Danny McCarthy) to destroy all the evidence. Catherine, hellbent on learning who killed her friend Isabel (Larissa Campos), quietly enters the greenhouse to confront Emma, who shoots her. But even injured, Catherine is beginning to remember things. When Alice arrives, Catherine says, “You wanted me to come here because you wanted me to kill him,” to which Alice replies, “We don’t get to decide what someone’s punishment will be.” That’s when Catherine delivers the monologue that seemingly changes Alice’s mind on that issue, as Catherine describes how she felt when killing the men who enabled their alpha, Jay Easton. “When I’m killing him, it’s like I’m eating him,” Catherine says, as Alice listens intently on the other side of the wall, mirroring her. “Like, I’m swallowing him, like everything he’s ever done is disappearing inside me, and I have all the fucking power in the world, and they don’t want us to have that. They wanna take that from us. But I want you to feel it.” Courtesy of Disney Armed with a handgun, Catherine goes upstairs into Jay’s secret room and finds Emma there, but Alice stops her from shooting. That’s when Catherine’s memories flood back, and she remembers that it was she who killed Isabel that night, injecting her with drugs — which ended up being her M.O. with all of her recent victims too. But with Isabel, Catherine was only speeding up the inevitable. After a horrible night spent with Easton and his friends, Isabel was in immense pain and had begun to bleed out — a complication from recently giving birth. “She asked me to,” a devastated Catherine tearfully tells Alice, as Alice cuffs her and they hold hands. Outside, Nora (Quincy Tyler Bernstine) is busting Ed for having colluded with Jay all these years, and he yells, “It was one dead girl! And she would have died anyway.” Alice slips into Jay’s room, and we see this scene play out for the first (but not last) time. “You’re the movie star!” Jay tells her, half-asleep. “I like your video. It was always one of my favorites.” In this version of the scene, Alice doesn’t have time to wonder what he means. He starts to cough, and Alice calls for help — but, as Nora later puts it, “No hard drives. No evidence. And he’s dead.” The rest of the finale unfolds from there: Nora attempts to get Danny (Scoot McNairy) to give her the evidence that Alden (Steve Way) slipped to him, we learn that Alice has been suspended and we see Alice and Danny meet up at the Jersey Shore in the freezing cold. “I can’t be rough with you,” Danny tells Alice gently as they tentatively begin an intimate relationship. “You know that.” He also says he’s going to retire — and then gives her the flash drive from Alden, which is full of child pornography Easton had saved. In another scene, as Nora and Alice watch Isabel’s body being moved from unmarked grave on Hart Island to an actual cemetery, Alice hands over the drive. But Nora’s triumph is short-lived after Alice tells her, “I’m on there too. I was 14. And I thought I was in love. And there’s a video. And Jay Easton had it.” Nora asks Alice whether she’s seen it, and when Alice says no, Nora says: “Why not? You want to do this job, you face it.” Related Stories 'The Witcher' Co-Producer Rae Benjamin to Receive Starz #TakeTheLead Award at Humanitas Event, Presented by Russell T Davies Shannon Wallace, Curtiss Cook, Lauren E. Banks, Liv Symone, Jason Dirden Join Starz Black Rodeo Drama When Nora gives Alice the code to the evidence room in the C20 unit, Alice does exactly that, searching her own name and learning that the video of her has been downloaded 50,042 times. This scene has been intercut with Alice’s visit to Catherine in jail, when Catherine says to Alice, “You have a secret.” Which is when we really see what happened to Jay Easton, as Alice not only steps on his breathing tube, but puts her hand over his mouth until he suffocates to death. “I said , did you like the way it felt?” Catherine asks Alice. Alice gives a split-second grin, and the show cuts to black, as Season 1 of “Furious” comes to an end. Left to right: Scoot McNairy, Emmy Rossum, Quincy Tyler Bernstine, Elizabeth Meriwether Courtesy of Disney Here, Rossum and Meriwether break down the finale in an interview that took place before Hulu officially renewed the show. When asked by Variety if she was already writing a second season, Meriwether began doing a robot dance. Then, when pressed, Meriwether said: “You can write: ‘She responded by doing a robot dance.’” Emmy, it was your idea as executive producer to adapt the 1987 Debra Winger movie “Black Widow” to adapt, though “Furious” became quite a different story. What elements from the original movie inspired you? Emmy Rossum: Women. Women! Check. The elevator pitch is: a female FBI agent hunting a female serial killer. I’m immediately leaning in. It starts very cat-and-mouse, and this character is in this very misogynistic workplace, and everybody’s doubting her — and that feels relevant, even today. Sad we have to say that. But the second half of the movie becomes this intimate character piece of this connection between these women. Liz, you hadn’t written a thriller before. What was your approach to adapting it? Elizabeth Meriwether: I was very scared of it. Like, how do I do this? I was just really fascinated by what a female serial killer’s history would be, and the psychology of a female serial killer. Especially in my old age, my way into a lot of my projects is research. I talked to a homicide detective, I read books about serial killers, and I spoke to an assistant district attorney and some FBI agents. The more I talked to people, the less intimidating it became to write a quote-unquote thriller — because I realized this is a story about people. As opposed to mapping out everything, and knowing when to put clues in the right place. All of that stuff was challenging, and came later. Catherine’s motivations are totally different from the movie. Meriwether: There are no motivations in the movie, which I think is really interesting for the time period. That movie would not be made nowadays, because there is such a need from executives to explain everything about why people are doing things. I use words like “tone poem” — it’s a movie that is a feeling, in a very cool way. And there’s even a really interesting scene where Debra Winger’s character gives a fake monologue about why she is the way she is, and then pulls a rug out from it. I love that about the movie, but you can’t do just cat-and-mouse for eight episodes. Courtesy of Disney If Jay is Jeffrey Epstein, that makes Emma his Ghislaine — except worse because she’s his daughter, and we see some very creepy boundary-crossing between them. Meriwether: That character was the hardest character to write for me. Hope was incredible in going on the journey with me and Cory Finley, who directed Episodes 7 and 8. I still don’t really think we answer the questions that I have about some of the women around these men — that is the part of it that confounds me the most. I have a lot of questions about the women who enable these men, and I don’t think we come up with a definitive answer. Courtesy of Disney Emmy, as Alice gets more invested in the case, is she allowing herself to acknowledge that she identifies with Catherine? Rossum: By letting Catherine go, she knows that she’s taking a huge risk, but she knows that she needs to do that. And she already has such a fluid relationship with protocol, right? The closer that she gets to Catherine, the more is woken up inside her that has been subconsciously and intentionally repressed. She remembers everything that happened to her, unlike Catherine. But I think that she has disconnected from that — that’s her survival mechanism. She wants to do this job. But you can tell from the first episode, her eyes are on that keypad. She wants to get in that room. She knows, at least in my belief, that there is this tape out there that could be in that room, and it’s this thing that’s been eating away at her. And this opportunity to go work at this FBI office and potentially get in there is not just because she has this burning desire to get justice for others, but also because she’s wondering if this tape is out there. Who’s seen it, and what’s to be done about that? The last shot of the finale is Alice’s smile after Catherine asks about her killing Jay Easton. How did you land on that as the final image, Liz? Meriwether: Was the smile in the script? [ Rossum nods. ] I was gonna give it all to you, Emmy. When I saw the first cut of it, I was like, “This is awesome .” That quick look. So yes, Emmy nailed it. And I honestly never looked at a different take. Courtesy of Disney Emmy, do you think Alice would have killed Jay had Catherine not told her that it feels like she has “all the fucking power in the world” in those moments? Rossum: I don’t think she went up there with the intention to kill him. I think Catherine has introduced this idea, right? Like, she says, “I know that there is a bit of you that wanted to kill Marshall. I know that there’s a bit of you that wants power.” They’re on opposite sides of the door; they’re literally mirroring each other. Then when Alice goes upstairs, seemingly to find Jay, he says that absolutely despicable thing to her, and I think the switch just goes. She’s like, “ Fuck this guy. Nora’s right: He’s gonna die peacefully in his bed.” Popular on Variety Meriwether: Hopefully, the show has taken her on that journey. In the first episode, Nora’s like, “Does it matter if Adrian Morado died? He was a bad man.” And Alice is like, “Of course it matters! That’s our job.” Alice is becoming Catherine, Catherine is becoming Alice. Catherine’s heart is opening up, and in some ways Alice is closing off, and getting darker and stronger. That was the dream. One thing that’s been driving Catherine is trying to find out how Isabel died. It turns out that she actually killed her. Was that always going to be the answer to that mystery? Meriwether: I mean, I wish I could tell you that I had it all planned from the beginning, but I really didn’t. I wrote the first two episodes, I didn’t know where it was going, and I just kept digging in and working on it, and then going back and rewriting. And then when that clicked in, you just get that feeling that that’s the right thing. Catherine stops being able to kill after she kills Hal [Campbell Scott] in Episode 5. She’s starting to get the feeling back in her fingers. She is starting to imagine having a life for herself, and not dying. Her heart is opening up. She’s getting her body back. So if she had figured out that somebody else had killed Isabel and then killed that person, I think that would have messed up the story we were trying to tell. And I found it really moving that to go on this mission of vengeance and then realize that you’re at the center of it — I don’t know. It stayed with me. And that’s how I knew it was right, because I couldn’t stop thinking about it. It felt really sad. Courtesy of Disney Emmy, can you talk about filming that scene with Lola Petticrew as Catherine’s remembering that night? Rossum: It was a long day. Lola and I — who actually never worked together that much — we are both very unguarded performers. We’re both like, unzip us, and here are our guts . You’re with another performer that approaches the material that Liz has written so unflinchingly and so raw, and these are two people who have been so closed off and who are really, really probably craving a friend, right? A female friend. We’ve seen Alice be so closed off from people, but also at moments with victims or witnesses, just have a real access to empathy that is not performative. There is this really deep connection between them. Meriwether: I rewrote it so many times, and I was so worried about that scene. Because also, as a comedy writer, writing a four-page scene where it’s just a person holding a gun, I was like, “What am I doing here? I should not be the person writing this!” I was really intimidated. Because it’s really just a series of monologues, and it’s a lot of dialogue. And you have to buy that everybody is scared, and that’s why they’re still there, and they still feel like Catherine could shoot somebody. You also have to buy that Alice cares enough about Catherine to want to help her get to this place. But I was just so blown away by all three of those women in that room that day watching them, because I felt — honestly, going into the day we were shooting it — guilty , because I was like, “I’m giving them an impossible task as actors to be able to pull this off.” I was so blown away by Lola’s ability to, as Emmy just said, unzip themselves and let out their heart and their guts. And then I was so blown away by Emmy — because the instinct in a lesser actor, I think, would be like to match Lola where Lola was. But Emmy kept it about Lola, and knew that her character’s moment was coming later in the episode. But it was just one of those just invigorating days as a writer, because you know the people you’re working with are just making it so much more . Catherine is in prison and married — I assume to Alden, even though they don’t say his name. Is that a happy ending for Catherine? Meriwether: I think what’s happy about it is that she’s alive. Her journey in my mind was that she is convinced that she’s doing this as a suicide mission. And then kind of her journey midway through is realizing that she actually wants to live, and Alice helps her get to that place where she feels like she actually wants to continue to live. So to me, that’s her ending place. Courtesy of Disney Can you both talk about where you feel we leave Alice at the end of the finale? Rossum: She has probably added a new secret to her arsenal of secrets. She enters C20 the first time with the secret of what’s in that room, which is her tape. And then gets on the squad, which is her mission the whole time, with a new secret, that she’s taken a life. When your worst fears are confirmed that that tape exists and that 50,000 people have watched your childhood trauma, I think there’s almost a peace at knowing you were right — and now, what do you do about it? And she got what she wanted, which was to get into that room and to get onto that squad. But I think that you know she’s on the next mission. Meriwether: I want to hear Emmy’s feelings about Alice always, because it’s so informative to me. I never felt like we should be fully rooting for violence from either character. And I do feel like Alice’s choice to kill Jay in the end is a choice that makes sense for the character and where she is. But I also question if going forward, that choice is something that traps her a little bit. Do you think that Alice would maintain a relationship with Catherine? Meriwether: I don’t know if we would get Lola back, honestly. I do think a hypothetical next season would pick up in C20 with Nora, working on a new case. Courtesy of Disney What’s in store for Alice and Danny, given what we know about what Alice has gone through? She just murdered a person. Meriwether: Well, you’re asking really good questions that I am asking myself, in my classic process where I don’t have a plan for the future. What happens in Season 1 works for Season 1 and the characters, and I’m trying to figure out what the future would be. And I don’t know yet! Rossum: I think he is wonderful and kind, but ultimately the character is limited in terms of the full scope of who she is, and how he could be with somebody that has that level of chaos and pain in their history? He’s very sensitive, and he said, “I don’t want to keep looking at that.” Like, “I gotta go.” And, of course, I identify so much with the character, and I’m so fused with her by this point that I’m, like, angry and trembling on her behalf just thinking about this imaginary relationship, you know? Like, how could you be in love with somebody, but actually love them so much that you can’t hold all of the pain that they have? When they can hold it just fine! Emmy, you’re down to keep playing Alice? Rossum: For as long as Liz will write her! This interview has been edited and condensed. Loading comments... title: ‘Onslaught’ Review: Adria Arjona and Dan Stevens Star in Adam Wingard’s Fun but Scattered Military Slasher
full_text: Aug 31, 2026 9:00am PT ‘Onslaught’ Review: Adria Arjona and Dan Stevens Star in Adam Wingard’s Fun but Scattered Military Slasher After two megabudget 'Godzilla vs. Kong' movies, the ‘Death Note’ director returns to his midnight indie roots in this A24 release. By Siddhant Adlakha Plus Icon Siddhant Adlakha Latest ‘Mustache’ Review: A Delightfully Anxious Pakistani American Coming-of-Age Comedy 4 weeks ago ‘Satluj’ Review: A Moving Indian Activist Drama Pulled From Circulation 1 month ago ‘Unidentified’ Review: Saudi Maverick Haifaa al-Mansour Crafts a Dull Murder Mystery 3 months ago See All Courtesy Everett Collection A 12-hour clock counts down to an inevitable massacre in “ Onslaught ,” the kind of elevated, razor-wire genre romp that director Adam Wingard and writer Simon Barrett used to make before studio outings like “Godzilla vs. Kong.” It isn’t the most polished of the duo’s output, and often feels in need of just another draft to tighten its nuts and bolts. But despite its occasional failings, this military-infused slasher thriller is their most aesthetically accomplished work, and a fun bookend to a jam-packed movie summer, before the transition to spooky season in the fall. Related Stories Shannon Wallace, Curtiss Cook, Lauren E. Banks, Liv Symone, Jason Dirden Join Starz Black Rodeo Drama ‘Outlander: Blood of My Blood’ Season 2 Trailer: Scottish Uprising Threatens 'Outlander' Prequel A trailer park for U.S. army veterans plays host to Adria Arjona ’s paranoid, gun-toting Celeste, a former sniper and the compound’s manager. Her continued target practice is plagued by black-and-white memories of war, but she’s soon interrupted when her well-to-do ex-husband shows up out of the blue to drop off their conscientious daughter Daisy (an adorable Blake Kennedy). As Celeste tries to keep the young tyke entertained, events at a covert military base nearby threaten her hard-earned domestic normality. Popular on Variety These strange happenings take the form of a markedly different, often more exciting movie that doesn’t actually cross paths with the mother-daughter drama until quite late into the 92-minute runtime. In a more heightened setting, the heavily made-up German scientist Dr. Hans Kammler ( Dan Stevens ) and his domineering wife Hanna (Rebecca Hall) complete their bunker experiments on a trio of sociopathic super-soldiers for a private military contractor. The film’s snappy opening montage, which goes backward in time through several American wars, maintains a particular focus on Operation Paperclip, hinting at Kammler’s Nazi ties as he details his torturous methods on his human weapons — at least two of whom are Black. (The third’s face is intentionally obscured.) These racial undertones don’t rise to the surface, nor are they meant to, given the language in which Wingard trades: that of the U.S. military industrial complex fueling horror-tinged imagery, à la his Halloween-meets-The Terminator delight “The Guest.” Social themes inform the plot, but are backgrounded in favor of gory, whizzbang action. Soon, the trio of ruthless slashers begins shooting and hacking their way through innocent towns with inventive weapons, until eventually — much, much, later — they make their way to Celeste’s inadvertent stronghold, where she makes her stand alongside her wise neighbor, Josiah (Reginald VelJohnson) and the slapstick local sheriff, Kovacks (Eric Wareheim). All the while, a clean-up crew led by Drew Starkey’s kinky, idiosyncratic hit man Cyrus follows close behind, but this is a third, more vestigial movie, which only distracts from the main event. The delayed gratification of the eponymous blitz has its pros and cons. On the one hand, the lengthy drama works to create proximity between Celeste and the viewer: Arjona’s rankled, hard-as-nails performance endears itself to us, sputtering with hints of warmth when she lets herself be protective and maternal. On the other, this also means that the zombified, camo-sporting villains — with their glowing eyes, and shapeless forms against the night sky — peak early with their inventive kills, forcing the climactic standoff to unspool through repetitive beats. These enhanced soldiers are meant to be super-smart, but this tends to go out the window so they can adopt the flailing cadence of Leatherface from “The Texas Chain Saw Massacre.” It’s isn’t a plot hole worth obsessing about — or a plot hole at all; combining war movies with horror iconography is clearly Wingard’s M.O. — but it does require a re-adjustment of expectations, owing to lessened stakes. Still, when you have a defenseless child in the mix, and a mother willing to go to great lengths to protect her, what you’re left with is bound to be a good time, especially as Wingard and composer Matthew Pusti pluck on your nerves with their taut audiovisual assembly. Whatever its structural misfortunes, “Onslaught” is counter-balanced by enough midnight verve and visceral violence to make it just about worthwhile. ‘Onslaught’ Review: Adria Arjona and Dan Stevens Star in Adam Wingard’s Fun but Scattered Military Slasher Reviewed at Dolby Screening Room, New York, Aug. 25, 2026. title: Watch ‘One In A Million’ Trailer, Oscar Contender That Follows Incredible Journey Of Syrian Girl Across Tumultuous Decade

The film from Frontline Features , PBS Distribution, and BBC Storyville follows Israa from the age of 11 until 21, a decade in which she fled the decimated Aleppo, Syria of her birth, arrived with her family in Turkey, then eventually made it to Germany as one of a million Syrian refugees admitted to that country. The odyssey, which involved incredible peril on the Mediterranean in an inflatable raft, and a brutal journey on foot through Eastern Europe, might remind one of a certain hero from Greek myth (and indeed a mooring on the Greek Island of Samos became a critical stop along the way). Related Stories Documentary DOC NYC Set To Honor Documentary Visionaries Alex Gibney, JT Takagi, Stephen Maing, And Raney Aronson-Rath Documentary Award-Winning 'One In A Million' Makes European Premiere At Thessaloniki Doc Fest Ahead Of CPH:DOX Bow We can share the first trailer for the film above, ahead of the film’s theatrical release in October. Watch on Deadline Israa in ‘One in a Million’ Frontline Features/BBC Storyville After the fall of the Assad regime in Syria, Israa like other Syrian exiles could weigh whether to return. For Israa the decision involved a reckoning with the opportunities afforded in Germany but a lingering sense that true fulfillment might be found back home. “Co-directors Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes bring a palpable blend of sensitivity and nuance to their portrayal of the Syrian refugee Israa and her loved ones, following them across time, borders, and shifting circumstances,” the Sundance program wrote. “It is clear that the filmmakers fully realize the weight of the trust and privilege that comes with undertaking a longitudinal project: to witness the experiences, challenges, and quiet joys of a remarkably resilient family forced to leave their beloved Aleppo.” Frontline Features/BBC Storyville Co-director Itab Azzam is a Syrian native herself. She and MacInness, her filmmaking and life partner, were living in Damascus in 2011 when Syria’s civil war broke out. “We left for London in August of that year planning to return a few months later, but that day never came,” they write in a directors’ statement. “Four years later in 2015, we met Israa selling cigarettes on a street corner in Turkey, as she and her family had just arrived from the devastation of Aleppo. Defiant and brimming with joy, despite the horror around her, we instantly fell in love with her – and felt that her story demanded telling… We knew we wanted to stay in her life. That was when the idea for One in a Million was born.” Directors Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes attend the 2026 Sundance Film Festival Awards Ceremony on January 30, 2026 in Park City, Utah. Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images One in a Million is directed and produced by Itab Azzam and Jack Macinnes and produced by Oscar winner Raney Aronson-Rath ( 20 Day in Mariupol ), Will Anderson, James Bluemel, and Andrew Palmer. Executive producers include David Fialkow and Nina Sing Fialkow, Harriet Gugenheim, Lucie Kon, Jutta Krug, Adam Lewis, Melony Lewis, Patty Quillin, Patty Quillin, and Joseph Schull. title: Could the Galliano Met Gala Fiasco Mark the End of Anna Wintour’s Reign?
full_text: × Skip to main content By Merle Ginsberg Plus Icon Merle Ginsberg View All August 31, 2026 8:46am Anna Wintour with John Galliano. Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images Every first week of May for the past 31 years, Vogue ’ s Anna Wintour has presided over the Costume Institute’s annual exhibit at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, and the accompanying Met Gala , the lavish, star-studded event that has become the fashion world’s equivalent of the Oscars. Now, with the withdrawal of the Costume Institute’s latest honoree , John Galliano , over controversy surrounding past racist and antisemitic comments, and the canceling of the exhibit , that hallowed 70-year-old tradition may be going on an embarrassing hiatus. (The Met, in a statement earlier this morning, said plans for a new exhibit and gala would be announced later.) Related Stories Lifestyle John Galliano Bows Out, Met Gala Exhibit Canceled Amid Backlash Lifestyle Met Gala Organizers Reportedly Mulling Date Change Amid John Galliano Backlash For Wintour, who at 76 has outlasted generational rivals like Graydon Carter and Tina Brown and has amassed unparalleled power at Condé Nast — the publisher of Vogue as well as titles like Vanity Fair, GQ and The New Yorker — the misstep may cause more than temporary embarrassment. Galliano, the longtime creative head of both Dior and Margiela — now collaborating with Zara — announced the news himself on Instagram Monday morning: “After much reflection and discussion with all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time. I do not want the debate surrounding me to place the Met in a difficult position or to distract from the remarkable work of the Costume Institute. I also recognize and respect that an exhibition my work would be painful for some.” This is quite a break with fashion precedent. No Met honoree has ever bowed out before, nor has any pre-announced theme been canceled. (Only two honorees, Yves-Saint Laurent in 1983 and Rei Kawakubo in 2017, were alive at the time of the exhibits devoted to their work; and Galliano was set to be the third living honoree.) But the Galliano choice was fraught the minute it was announced this summer. Despite his fashion genius, the notorious 2011 incident at a Paris — caught on a video, in which the visibly drunk designer slurred racist epithets to Jewish customers, declaring a fondness for Hitler and telling them their ancestors would be “gassed” — got him fired from Dior, making him an international persona non grata. Despite apologies (a very public one in his 2024 doc High and Low: John Galliano ) and work with Jewish leaders over the years, the rise of antisemitism in the last decade has brought the unfortunate — and inebriated — moment to the forefront. Wintour said Monday in a statement in support of Galliano as he headed for the exit: “John’s decision that the exhibition devoted to his work should not take place at this time is very courageous and a measure of the man he is. I believe this is the right decision, and both he and the Museum have my full support.” How bad was the backlash? Among the voices decrying the Met’s decision to lionize Galliano is New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has recently faced uproar over his vociferous criticism of Israel, which some have characterized as encouraging antisemitism. A spokesman for Mayor Mamdani last night shared the following statement with the New York Times : “John Galliano’s repeated use of antisemitic language is vile. The Mamdani administration recognizes that the Met’s decision to honor him has caused pain and anger among many Jewish New Yorkers. The Met is an independent institution and its decisions — and how it responds to the many Jewish New Yorkers appalled by this choice — are ultimately its own. But independence does not mean insulation from criticism.” Is Galliano to blame? Hardly. The designer simply accepted the honor from Wintour and Met Costume Institute chief curator Andrew Bolton, who’d prepared for some backlash by working with Galliano to preempt the inevitable criticism. Wintour clearly knew the risks, but perhaps underestimated them. Nor did she seem to be sufficiently prepared for the populist backlash the Gala received when she asked Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sanchez Bezos to co-chair/sponsor this year’s Ball to the tune of $10 million. New York streets were plastered with posters calling for a boycott of the gala, castigating the couple over their conspicuous displays of wealth, their lavish Venice wedding, Amazon’s $40 million Melania doc currying favor to the Trump administration and accusing them of attempting to buy their way into fashion high society. Marie Antoinette was invoked in some Bezos headlines, referring to Wintour. So how will Wintour deal with this onslaught of negative press? Some New Yorkers believe this finally might be the moment the fashion world’s ultimate survivor steps away from her near 40-year career at Condé. “She’s used to being called an ‘ice queen,’” says one well-placed source in the high echelons of the New York fashion world. “But not to this level of bitter backlash.” THR

title: ‘The Girl in the River’ Review: Tiffany Haddish in a Police Procedural That’s Like a Failed TV Pilot From a Past Era
full_text: × Skip to main content By Frank Scheck Plus Icon Frank Scheck View All August 31, 2026 8:41am 'The Girl in the River' Courtesy of Samuel Goldwyn Films “Business and feelings, they don’t go well in this line of work,” comments a veteran criminologist in the new thriller written and directed by Brando Benetton. It’s the sort of hackneyed observation made by jaded cops since they’ve first been portrayed onscreen, and it’s emblematic of the cornucopia of familiar elements in The Girl in the River . Depicting a murder/kidnapping investigation conducted by the older cop partnered with, you guessed it, a younger rookie colleague, this is a movie you’ll swear you’ve seen before. Devon Sawa ( Final Destination ) plays the cop, Alan Kramer, whose constant furtive sips from his liquor flask instantly let us know that he’s deeply troubled — in this case by the death of his young son, whose photograph he carries around and periodically stares at plaintively. His new partner, Amelia Pembrock ( Maggie Grace , the Taken movies), was the top-ranked cadet in her class, but her fear of actually going out in the field has led her to sabotage her own career. Related Stories News Tiffany Haddish Pleads Guilty to Misdemeanor Drunk-Driving Charge in Georgia TV 'Backyard Baseball' to Be Adapted as an Animated TV Series Starring Tiffany Haddish The Girl in the River The Bottom Line Dead in the water. Release date : Friday, September 4 Cast : Maggie Grace, Devon Sawa, Tiffany Haddish, Ralph Macchio, Andrew Stevens Director-screenwriter : Brando Benetton 1 hour 32 minutes So naturally this mismatched pair is recruited by a tough-talking, small-town police captain ( Tiffany Haddish , understated in a rare dramatic role) to investigate the murder of a teenage girl whose body was found in the Mississippi River and whose twin sister is missing. And in case we question the seriousness of the assignment, at one point the captain demands, “Close the case, no matter the cost!” Kramer, who’s on the verge of retirement, doesn’t want to take the case but he changes his mind after talking to the victim’s father (veteran actor and B-movie producer Andrew Stevens, who handles both chores here), a local politician and very big deal in the very small town. And so it goes, with the investigators working off such obscure clues as the victim’s teeth having been damaged post-mortem and raw chicken found under her fingernails. The latter leads to a prime suspect, a nebbishy local butcher who cares for his elderly mother and who seems exactly the type you’d think would murder a young girl. In an attempt to make the case against him, Pembrock commits a stunning act of illegality that would immediately have the case thrown out of court but at least provides the film a few moments of suspense. Helping the cops is an affable coroner played by Ralph Macchio , whose ever-likable presence should help with the film’s streaming numbers. The Girl in the River plays entirely by the book, by which I mean that there’s not a plot development you don’t expect, including the eventual reveal of the actual killer. (C’mon, you didn’t really think it was the butcher, did you?) The ensuing tense encounter includes one of the more unconvincing shootouts ever committed to film, although to be fair, two of the characters involved clearly have little prior experience. Making his feature directorial debut, Benetton delivers reasonably effective atmospherics but remains hamstrung by his script that seems to have been written by AI. Burdened by clichéd plotting and dialogue, the sluggishly paced film at least benefits from its two leads, who undertake their assignments with professionalism. A grizzled and gaunt Sawa invests his character with haunted, intense physicality, while Grace proves appealing in her Clarice Starling-like role. But their efforts are not enough to prevent the film from feeling like a failed TV pilot from a past era. title: Producer Peter Saraf Named Chair Of NYU Tisch’s Undergraduate Film And Television Department
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Mike Fleming Jr Mike Fleming Jr Editor-At-Large @DeadlineMike More Stories By Mike Patricia Clarkson Joins Tom Hanks & Callum Turner In Sony’s ‘The Comebacker’ Netflix Buys ‘Wingmom’ Film Spec By ‘Ghosts’ Co-EP Sam Laybourne Sony’s 3000 Pictures & Temple Hill Land ‘Dolly All The Time’ With Gemma Burgess Set To Adapt View All August 31, 2026 8:00am Peter Saraf Jenae Neeson / Courtesy Sundance Institute EXCLUSIVE : New York University’s Tisch School of the Arts on Monday appointed Peter Saraf as Chair of the Undergraduate Film and Television Department. After forging a career producing such films as Little Miss Sunshine and A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood , this is new terrain for Saraf, a place he hasn’t been since he earned his bachelor’s degree as a theater major at Wesleyan University. School starts today, and so does Saraf. What he lacks in academic bona fides, Saraf brings in more than three decades of experience producing film, television and theater. In addition to being chair, he will be an associate professor in the department and will continue to shepherd his current slate of projects while developing new ones. Related Stories News Sundance Stalwarts Peter Saraf & Eddie Rubin Launch Optimistic Pictures; Awkwafina Pic 'G' Among Their Early Projects News Netflix Acquires Animated Sundance Film 'White Fang' Saraf has produced more than 35 feature films, four episodic series and several theater productions to date. Aside from Little Miss Sunshine and A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood, his producing credits include The Farewell, Away We Go, Loving, Everything Is Illuminated, Land and Safety Not Guaranteed , as well as the series Nuclear Family, Vida and Sorry for Your Loss . He began his career working with Jonathan Demme and Edward Saxon on films including Beloved, Adaptation and Ulee’s Gold , as well as the documentaries The Agronomist and Mandela . He went on to co-found the independent producing and financing company Big Beach, which he ran for nearly two decades. Watch on Deadline Beyond his production work, Saraf has been an active leader within the industry, having served two terms as Vice President of the PGA and on the Executive Committee of the Producers Branch of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, as well as on the operating committee of Producers United, and on the boards of directors of the Future Film Coalition and the Woodstock Film Festival. Producing has always been an uphill climb, and it has been made steeper as the business roils with cutbacks and contraction and the infiltration of AI. Saraf saw Tisch as a place to share his experience in initiating projects and seeing them through to completion. “When they called, and my first thought was, why me, I’m not an academic,” Saraf told Deadline. “One of the things that appealed to me was, if I was going to go into academia, it would be good to come at it in a leadership role. I could bring those skills that I’ve built up over the years, being a producer and my experience running companies. It made me feel I could actually do something I know how to do in a meaningful way.” The Tisch Undergraduate Film and Television Department enrolls more than 1,400 students and produces upwards of 6,000 projects each year through a hands-on, “learn by doing” curriculum. “What stood out to me in Peter’s candidacy was not only the breadth of his experience, but the quality of his leadership — collaborative, measured, and forward-looking,” said Rubén Polendo, Dean of NYU Tisch School of the Arts. “He has demonstrated an ability to bring people together across different perspectives while maintaining a clear sense of direction, and he is uniquely positioned to guide the department at this pivotal moment, and to help shape its next chapter.” “Even though I don’t come from academia, I think my experience producing and running companies has prepared me for leading this great film and TV program,” Saraf said. “When considering the job, I realized these young people are the future of the art form and business that I have devoted my professional life to and to have a hand in their development is an incredible gift. Producing is largely about recognizing talent and supporting and enabling that talent to create great work. I’ve been doing that one project at a time; at Tisch, I have the chance to do it one generation at a time.” Designer John Galliano Pulls Out Of Exhibit Amid Backlash ‘Coyote Vs.
